summary: This excerpt from Book 11 (part 40) of a fiction work shows a quarrel between Rebecca and her aunt Miranda Sawyer. Miranda scolds Rebecca for her flowers, finery and airs, and insults Rebecca's late father Lorenzo as a vain, foolish, shiftless man who squandered his wife's money and left seven children. Rebecca defends her father through tears and is sent to bed without supper, while her sister Jane rebukes Miranda for bad manners and bad religion, and Miranda is left troubled by her conscience.
one_line: Aunt Miranda scolds Rebecca and insults her late father Lorenzo, and Jane rebukes Miranda's manners during a thunderstorm.
key_facts: Miranda tells Rebecca to take the rose out of her dress and calls her flowers, frizzled hair, furbelows and airs like those of her 'Miss-Nancy father'.
Rebecca answers that she will mind quickly when spoken to and never leave the door unlocked again, but will not have her father called names.
Rebecca says her father was 'a p-perfectly l-lovely father' and that it is MEAN to call him Miss Nancy.
Miranda describes Lorenzo as a vain, foolish, shiftless man who spent Rebecca's mother's money and left her with seven children to provide for.
Rebecca sobs that it is 'something to leave seven nice children'.
Miranda orders Rebecca upstairs to put on her nightgown, go to bed and stay there until the next morning, with no sound until breakfast time.
Miranda tells Jane to take the dish towels off the line and shut the shed doors because a 'turrible shower' is coming.
Jane says she does not often speak her mind but that Miranda ought not to have said what she did about Lorenzo.
Jane notes that Aurelia always says Lorenzo was a good husband.
Miranda says that dead husbands are usually good ones, but that the truth needs an airing and Rebecca will never amount to a hill o' beans without having her father trounced out of her.
Jane remarks that Miranda's words were not good manners and not good religion.
The clap of thunder makes no peal in Miranda Sawyer's ears as loud as Jane's remark does on her conscience.
Rebecca climbs the back stairs wearily, closes her bedroom door, and takes off her beloved pink gingham dress with trembling fingers.
